assessment.nobel_worthiness: Combines the task and skill-biased-technology framework with credible empirical work on trade shocks, and has changed how economists and policymakers think about labour demand, wage inequality and the distributional costs of trade and automation. It has broad reach across labour, trade and public policy, and it sits well within the credibility-based empirical tradition.
assessment.attribution: Katz is credited for the supply-demand framing of the skill premium and for long-run evidence on wage structure. Autor is credited for the task approach and for the technology and polarisation evidence. Autor and Hanson are credited, with Dorn as a close co-author, for the local labour market evidence on import competition. The three-name cap forces Dorn out, which is a real attribution cost, and the task-model strand also has other key authors outside this list.
assessment.maturity: The core work dates from the 1990s through the 2010s and has been replicated, extended and debated for years. The framework is now well enough tested to judge, and the timing is ripe.
uncertainties: Dorn is omitted by the three-laureate cap even though he is a co-author of the import-shock work.
The long-run persistence of the trade-shock effects and the interpretation of polarisation are still debated.
The two strands, tasks and trade shocks, may be seen as separable contributions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Foundations of modern open-economy macroeconomics through intertemporal models, plus the exchange-rate disconnect and related puzzles. This is a textbook-level, field-defining contribution that shaped how central banks and international institutions analyse exchange rates, current accounts and policy spillovers.
assessment.attribution: Obstfeld and Rogoff are the natural pairing for the New Open Economy Macroeconomics and the puzzle-defining papers. Redux-style models also owe something to other authors, and the puzzle literature is collective.
assessment.maturity: Decades of influence and extensive empirical and theoretical follow-up. The field has had no prize in this area for some time.
uncertainties: The empirical resolution of the disconnect puzzles remains incomplete.
Rogoff also appears in another ballot entry, so there may be overlap in how his contributions are credited.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: A major body of theory on trade policy and endogenous determination of protection, which is the standard framework for political-economy models of trade. This ballot's discovery description covers only the policy strand. Their wider, jointly authored work on trade, innovation and growth would add to the case but is not the stated discovery here.
assessment.attribution: The Grossman-Helpman partnership is distinctive and clearly credited, with a joint book and a series of joint papers. Protection for Sale is the anchor contribution.
assessment.maturity: More than three decades of influence. The empirical tests of the protection-for-sale model are mixed but substantial.
uncertainties: Empirical support for the specific protection-for-sale mechanism is mixed.
It is unclear whether the committee would frame the prize around the political-economy strand or the broader growth and trade work.
Helpman appears in a second ballot entry, which may overlap in the credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework and its monetary-policy rules underpin the modern practice of inflation targeting and central banking, so the policy and intellectual impact is very large. Calvo pricing, interest-rate rules and the integrated analysis of policy are the pillars.
assessment.attribution: Attribution is the main difficulty. This is a large collective field with many plausible contributors (Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and others), and any three-person selection leaves out significant authors. Calvo, Taylor and Woodford each have a distinct and identifiable contribution.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with decades of use, though the framework's performance in the post-2008 and post-pandemic periods has been criticised and has pushed extensions.
uncertainties: Attribution is contested because of the number of credible contributors.
There is a risk of the committee viewing the framework as an evolving research programme rather than a settled discovery.
Recent inflation episodes affect how forecasting and policy performance are judged.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Systematic formal and empirical analysis of how constitutions, electoral rules, state capacity and political institutions shape fiscal policy and economic outcomes. It provides a coherent framework for the economics of politics and has a large following in both theory and empirical work.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the best-known pairing for constitutional and electoral-rule analysis. Besley has related work on state capacity and political agency, and the combined credit is plausible though the ballot merges related strands.
assessment.maturity: The work spans from the 1990s to now. Related institutions research has already been recognised by the Academy in recent years, which helps establish the field's standing but may make the committee cautious about another award nearby.
uncertainties: Recent recognition of institutions research may reduce the appetite for another award in a closely related area.
Causal identification in the cross-country constitutional evidence is weaker than in the theory.
The ballot spans theory, empirical work and state capacity, so the discovery is somewhat diffuse.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The alternating-offers bargaining model, and its extension to decentralised markets, is a standard building block in game theory, labour and search economics, and in the theory of contracts and negotiations. It is a clean, durable theoretical result with wide application.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein is the clear originator of the alternating-offers solution. Wolinsky is the natural co-author for markets. Binmore also contributed to the strategic bargaining approach, so there is a plausible case for a third name, but the cleanest credit goes to the first two.
assessment.maturity: Very mature, with four decades of use, which supports the judgment of lasting importance.
uncertainties: The importance of Binmore's contribution relative to the others may be argued.
Its empirical impact is more indirect than for the higher-ranked candidates.
Game theory has had several recent awards, which may affect relative priority.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Brings empirical estimates of behavioural responses, such as the elasticity of taxable income, together with the optimal-tax framework, so that tax-policy design rests on evidence. It is relevant to practical policy and to the large public-economics literature on taxation and redistribution.
assessment.attribution: Slemrod is credited with early work on taxable-income responses and tax avoidance. Saez is credited with the optimal-tax and top-income-response synthesis. Chetty is credited with the sufficient-statistics approach and with large administrative-data applications. Stantcheva, who is excluded by the cap, also has substantial work. The attribution is broad and partly overlaps with other ballot entries.
assessment.maturity: Fairly mature for Slemrod and Saez, and less settled for the newer sufficient-statistics and administrative-data strands. Identification of the taxable-income elasticity remains debated.
uncertainties: Identification and interpretation of the taxable-income elasticity remain contested, including mean reversion and income-shifting issues.
Saez and Chetty also appear in other ballot entries, so credit may overlap.
Stantcheva is excluded by the three-name cap.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Partial identification changed how researchers think about what data can and cannot reveal without strong assumptions, and so addresses credibility of inference and policy analysis directly. It has influenced econometrics, program evaluation and policy analysis.
assessment.attribution: Manski is the clear originator of the bounds approach. Tamer made central contributions to the moment-inequality and incomplete-model inference, with Molinari contributing in particular on inference and practical implementation. A single-name or two-name award around Manski would be easiest to defend.
assessment.maturity: Manski's foundational work is decades old, and the inferential machinery has matured over the last two decades. Applied adoption is more limited than for point-identification methods.
uncertainties: Applied uptake is narrower than for other econometric methods, which may weigh against it.
Econometric methods have been recognised recently, which may affect competition for this slot.
The relative credit between Manski and the later inference authors is uncertain.
